text:
**Tea Dance**

The first thing I learned about my father's life was its vocabulary. I was eight when he moved out of the house in Maplewood and into a fourth-floor walkup on West Twentieth Street. By nine I could tell you the difference between a bear and an otter, could point out from a taxi the bars on Eighth Avenue that had changed their names, and knew that when Uncle Gil said someone was "family" he did not mean they were related to us. I learned that "Mary" could be said to a man, and that it could mean anything from *Oh, please* to *I love you*. I learned that "positive" was not a good word, though no one ever said so.

My mother handled the divorce the way she handled everything, by pretending it had been her idea. She spoke of my father as you might of a man who had moved to Portugal: with distant respect for the boldness of the decision and no interest in the details. On alternate weekends my father met me under the clock at Penn Station, always early, always in the same camel-colored coat, always holding a hot chocolate gone lukewarm because he'd bought it too soon.

His apartment smelled of coffee and a cologne called Eternity, which I thought was the most romantic word I had ever seen on a bottle. He had a cat named Ethel, after Ethel Merman, and a poster of *Sunset Boulevard* in the bathroom, so that Gloria Swanson watched me brush my teeth. On Saturday mornings his friends came over for what they called brunch and what was, in practice, three hours of mimosas and gossip. There was Gil, large and bearded, who wept at commercials, and Raymond, who had been a dancer and still stood as if someone might photograph his feet. There was a rotating cast of younger men. And there was Luis, who had been my father's boyfriend, and then was not, and then was sick, and then, the winter I turned eleven, was a name the others said quietly, the way you'd set down a glass you weren't sure would hold.

I wanted badly to belong to them. The girls at school wanted to belong to each other, to the cluster that ate lunch near the windows. I could not have cared less. I wanted Raymond to tell me I had a natural turnout, and Gil to call me Mary. I wanted my father, when one of the younger men asked who I was, to say, "This is Tess. She's the best thing I ever did." He did say it, every time, so that I came to think of it as my full legal name.

So I studied. I memorized *Gypsy* and *Follies*. I learned Raymond's eye roll, a slow orbit ending at the ceiling as though God were in on the joke. I was an anthropologist who had gone native, except that the natives had never asked me to leave, and I had nowhere else I would rather have gone.

---

The cruise was my father's idea, though he presented it as Gil's. I was thirteen. He'd lost weight that winter, enough that his camel coat hung on him like something borrowed, and he'd had pneumonia in February, which my mother called "Daniel's chest thing." In March he pushed a glossy brochure across a diner table. On the cover was a white ship against a blue so saturated it looked like a printing error, and a headline in pink script: *Seven Nights. Four Islands. One Big Family.*

"It's a gay cruise," he said, unnecessarily.

"I can see that."

"Gil and Raymond are going. I'd like you to come. If your mother says yes." He turned his coffee cup a quarter turn on its saucer, a gesture I recognized as one of my own. "You won't be the only kid."

I asked why now, in April, when I'd miss a week of school.

He looked at me for a long moment, deciding how much to say. "Because I've always wanted to," he said. "And I'd like to do it with you."

My mother said yes. I think she knew what he wasn't saying and was too proud to say it either. On the morning I left she held my face in both hands and said, "Be good to him." It was not what I had expected.

---

The *Celestine* left Fort Lauderdale on a Saturday so hot the air seemed to have texture. In the terminal were perhaps eight hundred men, and the noise was like brunch amplified through a stadium. Old friends greeted each other with shrieks. Men alone with their suitcases looked around with the guarded hope of people arriving at a party where they might or might not be welcome.

I held my father's hand, which I had not done in public in years. His was cool and dry.

"Well," said Raymond, behind enormous sunglasses. "It's like Fire Island got lost at sea."

In our small cabin my father lay down for a nap almost immediately, and I sat on the floor reading the daily schedule. *Disco Bingo, Starlight Lounge, 8 p.m.* There was a theme for each evening, White Night and Prom Night among them, and on the last day something called the Captain's Farewell Tea Dance.

"What's a tea dance?" I asked.

He didn't open his eyes. "A dance in the afternoon. Back when it was illegal for men to dance together, they'd do it at the beach, in the afternoon, and call it a tea dance. So the police wouldn't come."

"Did they come anyway?"

"Sometimes." He reached out and found the top of my head without looking. "Mostly we were too early for them."

---

I had worried I would be in the way, a reminder of the world they had paid to escape. Instead I became a mascot. A pair of accountants from Chicago taught me gin rummy and let me win. A retired schoolteacher named Howard, who wore a captain's hat from home, appointed me first mate and gave me a whistle, which I blew at inappropriate moments to universal applause. On White Night, a drag performer called Miss Lorna Doone, six-foot-four in heels with the bone structure of a Roman emperor, did my eyeliner with a hand so steady it was like being drawn on by an architect.

"You've got your daddy's eyes," she said. "Sad and pretty. Don't waste them on boys who can't see."

"There aren't any boys," I said. "Well. There's one."

His name was Simon. He was fourteen, traveling with his father, a soft-spoken architect from Baltimore, and his father's partner, Theo, who laughed with his whole body. Simon stood at the edges of rooms reading paperbacks with the covers folded back. For three days we avoided each other with deliberate precision, each afraid the adults would push us together.

The adults did. On the third night Theo leaned across the dinner table and said, "Simon, why don't you show Tess the thing you found? On the top deck?" Simon turned the red of a stop sign.

"There's no thing," he said.

"There's a thing," said Theo serenely.

There was. He led me past a chain marked *CREW ONLY* to a platform behind a lifeboat. From there you could see the ship's wake spread out behind us in the dark, glowing faintly green.

"Bioluminescence," Simon said. "Plankton. When the ship churns them up, they light up."

We watched it for a while. Below us, faintly, came the bass line of the party.

"Your dad's sick," Simon said. Not a question.

I had never said it aloud. My father had never said it to me. He'd said *chest thing* and *a little run-down*. He had said *I'd like to do it with you*.

"Yes," I said.

The word came out with a strange lightness, like a stone I'd held in my mouth for years and finally let fall into the water.

Simon didn't say he was sorry, which I was grateful for. Instead he said, "My mom died when I was nine. Car accident." He picked at a flake of paint on the railing. "Everybody kept telling me how I should feel. Mostly I felt like I was in a play and nobody had given me the script."

I laughed, then worried laughing was wrong. But he was smiling too, a lopsided smile that changed his whole face.

"That's how I feel," I said. "All the time. Like I'm trying to learn my lines."

"You're good at it, though. Everyone loves you."

"They love me because I'm Daniel's daughter."

"They love you because you blew a whistle in the middle of the captain's toast," he said. "That was funny."

We stayed until the green faded and my arms were covered in goosebumps. We didn't kiss. We talked, the way I'd only ever talked to myself at night. He told me he wrote poetry and was ashamed of it. I told him I sometimes wished I were a boy, so I could be one of them without any asterisk. He didn't laugh. He said, "I think you already are one of them. Just the girl version." It was the nicest thing anyone had ever said to me.

When we came back down, my father was in a deck chair by the pool, wrapped in a towel though it was warm. He raised one eyebrow, a gesture he had taught me, or I had taught him.

"Well, Mary," he said. "Where have *you* been?"

---

The next days fanned out like cards. In Key West, Simon and I ate key lime pie on a stick on Duval Street. In Cozumel my father was too tired to leave the ship, so we played Scrabble in the empty dining room and he let me use *fabulosity*, which is not a word. In Grand Cayman, Gil cried on a sandbar among stingrays, and Raymond, for the first time I had ever seen, took off his sunglasses and stood in the water with his face turned up to the sky.

I noticed there were other men like my father on board: thin men, men in sweaters in the heat, men whose partners' hands rested lightly on their backs. Nobody asked them to explain. The shrieking, the sequins, the Disco Bingo were not the opposite of the illness but an answer to it. They were a refusal, a tea dance at the edge of the beach before the police could arrive.

On Prom Night, Simon wore a rented tuxedo short in the sleeves, and I wore blue taffeta Miss Lorna Doone had lent me, taken in with safety pins. We rated outfits from the edge of the dance floor. My father, in the camel coat he refused to stop wearing, got an eleven. Simon said that was cheating. I said it was the only accurate rating of the night.

---

The Tea Dance was held on the pool deck at four in the afternoon on the last day. The sea had gone flat and silver, as though someone had ironed it. For an hour the DJ played disco, and the deck moved like a single animal, hundreds of men singing along to Donna Summer. I danced with Gil, who spun me until I was dizzy. I danced with Raymond, who told me, finally, that I had a natural turnout. I danced with Simon, badly, both of us laughing, and when the song ended he squeezed my hand once and let it go.

My father had sat in the shade all afternoon. Around five the DJ slowed things down with Ella Fitzgerald singing "Someone to Watch Over Me," and the crowd thinned into couples. My father stood. It took him a moment. He walked across the deck toward me, and other men stepped aside, not in pity but in courtesy, the way you make room for someone carrying something fragile and important.

"May I have this dance?"

I put my arms around his neck. I could feel his shoulder blades, sharp as the edges of a book. He smelled of sunscreen and Eternity. We swayed with the ship, and I rested my head against his chest and listened to his heart. It was going steadily, as though it had all the time in the world.

"Did you have a good time, Tess?"

"The best time."

"Good." He was quiet a moment. "I wanted you to see this. Them. Us. Whatever happens, you belong here. You always did."

I wanted to say that I knew, that I had said it aloud to a boy on the top deck and it hadn't killed me. I wanted to say he was the best thing I ever had. But I was thirteen, and I didn't have the script. So I said nothing, and held on, and let Ella sing it for both of us.

Someone blew a whistle. Howard, probably, who had stolen it back that morning. A cheer went up, and my father laughed, a real laugh, and I felt it move through his body and into mine.

---

He died the following March at St. Vincent's, in a room facing the Hudson. Gil and Raymond were there, and so was my mother, who held his hand and called him Danny, a name I had never heard her use. The memorial was held in a bar on Eighth Avenue that had changed its name twice since I was a child. Miss Lorna Doone sang "Someone to Watch Over Me," and I wore the blue taffeta dress, which she had told me to keep.

Simon sent a card from Baltimore with a poem about green light in dark water. It wasn't very good. I have it still.

I am older now than my father was on that ship. I have stood at the edges of many rooms since, learning my lines. But I think often of that afternoon: the gold light, the silver sea, the men stepping aside. I think of the word he taught me without meaning to. Tea dance. A party held early, in daylight, in defiance. A way of saying: we were here, and we danced, and we got there before anyone could stop us.
